At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1768)
response:
Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive inference by having a small draft model propose k tokens that a larger target model then verifies in a single forward pass — the speedup depends entirely on the acceptance rate, the fraction of draft tokens the target model agrees with. The central question here is: when the input distribution shifts away from the domain the draft model was trained or calibrated on (e.g., moving from web text to legal contracts, or from English to code), does the acceptance rate degrade uniformly across all token positions in the draft sequence, or does it collapse preferentially at certain positions? The key concepts are draft-target KL divergence (how different the two models' next-token distributions are at any given context), positional compounding (errors at position i corrupt the context seen at position i+1, potentially cascading), and the distinction between marginal acceptance rate and its variance across positions. A beginner assumes acceptance rate is a stable scalar you can measure once and rely on; an expert worries that under domain shift the distribution of acceptance rates becomes heavy-tailed and position-dependent — the first one or two draft tokens may still look fine while later positions collapse, meaning your wallclock speedup estimate is both optimistic and highly sensitive to the specific domain mismatch in ways that are hard to detect without per-position instrumentation.

In the in-domain setting, optimal k is typically chosen by balancing the cost of a rejected suffix (wasted draft compute plus rollback overhead) against the expected number of accepted tokens — empirically landing around k=4–8 for systems like DeepMind's Medusa or Google's SpecBench evaluations, where acceptance rates of 0.7–0.9 make long drafts worthwhile. Under domain shift, compounding divergence means the marginal acceptance probability at position i is approximately α^i where α itself is now a function of domain distance — so if α drops from 0.85 to 0.60 due to shift, the expected accepted tokens from a length-8 draft falls from ~5.7 to ~2.1, and you're paying full draft compute for a fraction of the return. The non-obvious implication is that optimal k under shift isn't just "shorter" — it's that the optimum becomes sharper and more sensitive: the expected-speedup curve flattens and then falls off more steeply, so the penalty for over-specifying k grows disproportionately. Leviathan et al. (2023) showed that acceptance rate is the dominant term in the speedup formula, but they assumed stationarity; under domain shift you need a k that's robust to α variance, not just optimal at its mean. Practically, systems should treat k as a dynamic parameter estimated online via a sliding-window acceptance rate monitor per-position, rather than a static hyperparameter set at deployment — something production systems like vLLM's speculative decoding module have begun to support but don't yet do with per-position granularity.

With gradual domain shift, the sliding-window estimator's signal is dominated by recently-seen tokens that are only marginally more out-of-distribution than what came before, so the tracked acceptance rate declines slowly and smoothly — masking the fact that the cumulative drift has moved the operating point far from where k was calibrated. The false confidence problem is structural: a window of size W has a lag of roughly W/2 requests before it reflects the true current acceptance rate, and if the drift rate is slower than 1/W, the estimator never catches up — it perpetually reports a rate that corresponds to conditions from hundreds or thousands of tokens ago. This is directly analogous to concept drift detection failures studied in the streaming ML literature (Gama et al., 2014), where ADWIN and similar algorithms are known to have detection delays proportional to the inverse drift rate — slow drifts are the hardest case, not fast ones. The specific danger for speculative decoding is that the system continues using an over-long k with what appears to be a healthy acceptance rate of, say, 0.75, while the true current rate has silently fallen to 0.55 — the speedup has already evaporated but no alarm fires. Worse, because later draft positions compound error, the variance of per-request latency increases before the mean acceptance rate visibly drops, meaning latency tail behavior (p95, p99) degrades well before any scalar monitoring metric catches it — exactly the regime where SLA violations accumulate invisibly.

The natural candidate is a per-position variance statistic on acceptance indicators rather than their mean — specifically, tracking Var(A_i) across a window where A_i ∈ {0,1} is the acceptance at draft position i, since variance rises before the mean falls when a Bernoulli process drifts toward p=0.5 from either direction. A cleaner signal is the position-conditioned acceptance rate slope: fit a linear regression of acceptance rate against position index within each draft, and monitor the slope coefficient — under healthy in-domain conditions this slope is shallow, but under drift it steepens as later positions collapse faster, and the slope change precedes aggregate rate decline by roughly the window lag. The difficulty is that both statistics require per-position tracking across requests, which means your monitoring state is O(k) rather than O(1), and correlations between positions (because a rejection at position i terminates the draft, censoring observations at i+1 through k) introduce survivorship bias that makes naive variance estimates systematically overconfident — positions that are rarely reached look artificially healthy. This censoring problem is non-trivial: it's a variant of the truncated sequential observation problem, and correcting for it requires either inverse-probability weighting (reweighting late-position observations by the probability of reaching them) or a latent-variable model over full draft trajectories, neither of which is cheap to run online. Constructing this in a production system like TensorRT-LLM or vLLM would require instrumenting the speculative execution kernel at per-token granularity and piping that telemetry to a stateful monitor — currently neither system exposes this, meaning the early-warning signal that would actually help is precisely the one that existing infrastructure makes hardest to collect.

Deliberate over-extension is essentially a bandit exploration strategy applied to draft length, and it's worth framing precisely: you're paying a known cost (extra draft compute for positions k+1 through k+Δ, plus increased rejection probability) to gain an unbiased sample of late-position acceptance rates that censoring would otherwise hide. The conditions under which this is worth paying are: (1) the drift detection value — the expected cost of not detecting a shift early, integrated over the lag period — exceeds the per-request exploration overhead, and (2) the exploration can be amortized across enough requests that the signal-to-noise ratio on the probed positions is sufficient to actually update k meaningfully, which requires roughly 1/p(reach position k+Δ) samples for an unbiased estimate, growing exponentially if in-domain α is already moderate. In practice, if α=0.75 and you want to probe position k+4 beyond current k, you need on average (0.75)^{-4} ≈ 3.2 requests just to get one uncensored observation there — meaning you need hundreds of requests for a stable estimate, during which the domain may have shifted further. The right deployment pattern is therefore stochastic over-extension: with probability ε (say 0.05–0.10) extend by Δ=2–3 tokens, which keeps mean overhead low while accumulating late-position samples at a rate sufficient for drift detection on timescales of thousands of requests — analogous to epsilon-greedy exploration in contextual bandits, as studied in the online learning literature by Auer et al. (2002). The critical condition that makes this scheme not worth paying is when the target model's verification cost dominates draft compute, as in very large target models (e.g., 70B+ parameter models where a single forward pass is already the bottleneck) — there, the marginal cost of verifying extra draft tokens is negligible, so you should simply always over-extend and treat the extra positions as free probes.

The acceptance indicator A_i alone is indeed identical under both failure modes, but the rejected token distribution is not — when the draft model has diverged, rejected positions show the target model substituting tokens from a systematically different region of vocabulary (domain-appropriate tokens the draft never assigned high probability to), whereas target model uncertainty produces rejections where the target's own distribution is flat or multimodal, substituting tokens that are also low-probability under the target. Concretely, you can distinguish these by logging two quantities at each rejection: the target model's entropy H(p_target) at that position, and the KL divergence D_KL(p_draft || p_target) — high KL with low target entropy signals draft divergence, while high KL with high target entropy signals target uncertainty, and these have opposite remediation implications. This decomposition is related to the confidence-vs-calibration distinction in the uncertainty quantification literature, and Malinin & Gales (2018) formalize exactly this separation between distributional uncertainty (the draft is wrong) and model uncertainty (nobody knows) in the context of ensemble disagreement — the same logic applies here with draft and target as the two "ensemble members." The practical obstacle is that logging the full softmax distribution at every rejected position is expensive — a 100K vocabulary target model produces 400KB of float32 data per rejected token — so production systems would need to log only summary statistics (entropy, top-k probability mass, argmax confidence) rather than full distributions, accepting some loss of diagnostic resolution. A workable implementation would instrument the target model's verification pass to emit (H_target, p_target(draft_token)) pairs on rejections only, which are sparse enough to be cheap, and then cluster these pairs across a monitoring window to separate the two failure regimes without full distribution logging.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1774)
response:
When both failure modes are simultaneously active, naive remediation risks interference: lowering draft temperature to re-align with a diverged draft model reduces vocabulary diversity, which worsens outcomes in high-target-uncertainty regions where you actually need broader sampling to avoid the target repeatedly rejecting a confidently-wrong draft. The correct framing is a constrained optimization over adaptation budget — if you have signals (H_target, D_KL) decomposed per position as discussed previously, you can estimate the fraction of rejections attributable to each cause and allocate remediation proportionally, but the coupling between the two modes means the remediation effects aren't additive: fixing draft divergence by 50% and target uncertainty by 50% doesn't recover 100% of lost acceptance rate because the two interact at the token level. A principled approach treats this as a two-armed resource allocation problem where the "arms" are draft re-alignment (e.g., continued fine-tuning on recent accepted tokens, or switching to a domain-adapted draft model if one is available) and decoding adjustment (e.g., raising target sampling temperature or using nucleus sampling with adaptive p), with returns estimated from the per-mode rejection fractions — Pareto-optimal allocation sits where the marginal acceptance rate gain per compute dollar is equalized across both arms. The numbers matter here: if 70% of rejections are draft-divergence-driven and 30% are target-uncertainty-driven, spending adaptation budget entirely on draft re-alignment recovers roughly 0.7× of the theoretical maximum gain, but the residual 30% uncertainty-driven rejections now become more visible and may dominate the tail latency — meaning partial fixes can paradoxically make tail behavior worse by removing the masking effect of the larger draft-divergence signal. Google's work on online distillation for speculative decoding (Stern et al., 2018 and follow-ons) implicitly assumes draft divergence is the only failure mode, which is why those approaches work well on stationary distributions but lack a mechanism to handle the mixed case — the field hasn't yet produced a system that explicitly separates and co-optimizes both remediations simultaneously.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1775)

The bias is severe and has a specific structure: training the draft model only on accepted tokens is equivalent to minimizing KL divergence on a proposal-weighted subset of the data distribution, where the proposal is the draft model itself — this is a form of self-reinforcing feedback where the draft becomes increasingly confident on tokens it already handles well while the unobserved rejected regions atrophy further, analogous to the reward hacking failure mode in RLHF documented by Gao et al. (2023) where optimization against a proxy signal collapses diversity. Quantitatively, if the draft accepts at rate α=0.7, then 30% of token positions — systematically the hardest ones under domain shift — contribute zero gradient signal, and because these are the positions with highest D_KL(p_draft || p_target), they're exactly where adaptation is most needed; the effective training distribution is missing its most informative tail. The correction that doesn't require the full target distribution is importance weighting on rejected tokens using only the substitute token the target model emits at rejection — you observe the target's argmax (or sample) at rejected positions for free as part of the speculative decoding protocol, and this single token is an unbiased draw from p_target, sufficient to construct a one-sample importance-weighted gradient estimate for the draft model at that position. This one-sample estimator has high variance — you're estimating a distribution from a single draw — but it's unbiased, and in expectation over many rejections it correctly reweights the draft's loss toward the underrepresented tail; the variance can be controlled by capping importance weights (clipping at some maximum ratio, as in PPO's clipped surrogate from Schulman et al. 2017) without reintroducing the original bias. The deeper problem is that even with this correction, the contexts leading to rejected positions are themselves biased — you only reach position i if positions 1 through i-1 were accepted, so the context distribution seen during online adaptation is smoother and more in-domain than the true context distribution the draft will face after adaptation shifts its behavior, creating a second-order distributional mismatch that the one-sample correction doesn't address.
